entries.title: IEA: solar PV was the biggest source of energy demand growth in 2025, and battery storage additions rose about 40%
entries.summary: The IEA's Global Energy Review 2026 says solar PV met more than 25% of the rise in global energy demand in 2025, added a record 600 TWh of generation, and battery storage capacity additions reached almost 110 GW.
points: Global energy demand growth slowed to 1.3% in 2025; solar PV met more than 25% of the increase, the first time a modern renewable has been the largest source of demand growth.
Solar PV generation rose by 600 TWh, the largest one-year increase by any source outside post-crisis recovery periods, covering around 70% of electricity generation growth.
Renewable capacity additions rose to a record 800 GW, of which solar was 75%; battery storage additions rose by around 40% to almost 110 GW.
Electricity demand grew nearly 3%, well over twice the rate of overall energy demand; in the EU, solar and wind reached 30% of generation, above fossil fuels for the first time.
entries.plain_tip: In plain terms: in 2025 solar added more new electricity than any other source, and batteries were the fastest-growing power technology.
entries.caution: Figures are quoted from the publisher and may be revised in later editions. For understanding the market only; not investment or trading advice.

entries.title: EU CBAM definitive regime: in force since 1 January 2026 for six sectors including electricity and hydrogen
entries.summary: The European Commission says the CBAM definitive regime applies from 1 January 2026: EU importers above a 50-tonne threshold must become authorised CBAM declarants, buy CBAM certificates, and surrender them for embedded emissions each year.
points: Applies from 1 January 2026 to imports of cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen.
Importers (or their indirect customs representatives) bringing in more than the single mass-based threshold of 50 tonnes of CBAM goods per year must apply for authorised CBAM declarant status.
The certificate price follows the EU ETS auction price (€/tonne CO2): a quarterly average in 2026 and a weekly average from 2027.
Importers declare the emissions embedded in imports and surrender the corresponding certificates each year; a carbon price already paid in the producing country can be deducted if proven.
entries.plain_tip: In plain terms: goods that enter the EU have to carry the same carbon price as goods made inside the EU.
entries.caution: This is a summary of the Commission's overview page, not legal advice; thresholds, default values and deadlines are set in the legal texts and can be amended. Check the Commission's CBAM pages before acting.

entries.title: US wind and solar tax credits: the 4 July 2026 start-of-construction deadline has passed, and the IRS notice on how to prove it was vacated by a court
entries.summary: Under the OBBBA, wind and solar facilities placed in service after 31 December 2027 lose the 45Y/48E credits unless construction began on or before 4 July 2026. On 6 June 2026 the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia vacated IRS Notice 2025-42 in full and sent it back to the IRS; the court's memorandum opinion was read for this entry.
points: The OBBBA ends the Section 45Y production credit and Section 48E investment credit for applicable wind and solar facilities placed in service after 31 December 2027, unless construction began on or before 4 July 2026 (court opinion, Background; IRS Notice 2025-42, section 1).

IRS Notice 2025-42 (issued 15 August 2025) made the Physical Work Test the only way to show construction began for wind and most solar, and kept the Five Percent Safe Harbor only for solar projects of 1.5 MW or less (opinion, Background, citing Notice sections 3.01 and 6.02).

In Oregon Environmental Council v. IRS, No. 25-4400 (CKK), the court held the Notice arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act because the IRS gave no reasoned explanation for removing the safe harbor and did not weigh reliance on the earlier policy (opinion, Part III.E).
The remedy was to vacate Notice 2025-42 in full, not only for the plaintiffs, and remand to the IRS; two of the seven plaintiffs (HUC and OPC) were dismissed (opinion, Parts III.F and IV).
The court noted that the IRS could adopt new guidance on remand and that appeal rights would extend past 4 July 2026. Events after 6 June 2026 were not verified from the docket for this entry.
entries.plain_tip: In plain terms: the start-building deadline for the old US wind and solar credit rules was 4 July 2026; a federal court struck down the IRS notice that tightened how to prove it, and the IRS may issue new guidance.
entries.caution: This is a short summary of a court opinion, not tax or legal advice. The legal status may have changed after the opinion (appeal, new IRS guidance); check the court docket and IRS guidance and ask a qualified adviser.
